citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley / UChicago)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, and a final boxed answer. Problems are tagged by difficulty level (1–5) and span seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:annotatorDemographics: Human evaluators for the human-level performance study were six university students studying computer science. Four were authors on the paper; the other two were friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. Participants were offered remuneration but volunteered. The study was conducted by the Steinhardt Group at UC Berkeley.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems in MATH are curated from competition mathematics (AMC, AIME, etc.) and come with step-by-step solutions and final boxed answers as created by the competition mathematics community. For human evaluation, participants had one hour to complete 20 randomly sampled problems from the MATH test set, without using a calculator. Difficulty levels (1–5) follow AoPS conventions.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems are written in LaTeX and natural language, with figures encoded in the Asymptote vector graphics language.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging even for humans: a computer science PhD student attained approximately 40% accuracy, and a three-time IMO gold medalist attained 90%. Large language models achieve only 3.0%–6.9% accuracy, indicating the benchmark may be too hard for current models to show meaningful differentiation. The authors note that simply scaling Transformer models is unlikely to solve MATH in the foreseeable future, requiring new algorithmic advancements.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions encoded with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent fraction encodings, parenthesis encodings, units, spaces, and common equivalent number representations are normalized for exact-match evaluation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would have ramifications for cheating on homework. They explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. The dataset is intended to help the research community better forecast and improve reasoning capabilities of ML models.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; forecasting reasoning capabilities of ML systems. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to be used to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: None. The dataset consists entirely of mathematics competition problems and solutions with no personal or sensitive information.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The dataset problems come with solutions from competition sources; no independent annotation count per item is described.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality analysis is described; problems come pre-solved from competition sources.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No annotation platform used; problems are sourced directly from competition mathematics community. Human evaluation was too small (6 participants) and informal to constitute a platform-based annotation effort.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: No explicit bias acknowledgements or bias-mitigation design decisions are discussed for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the MATH dataset collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is stated, only that competitions span decades.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; dataset consists of complete competition problems with solutions.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection manipulation (augmentation, balancing, resampling) described for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools used in the MATH dataset creation; problems are sourced from competitions with human-written solutions.
